audience.programmeDescription: Psychobiology at UvA studies how biological processes in the brain and body relate to cognition, emotion and behaviour. Two compulsory years develop biology, neuroscience, psychology and research skills, followed by open electives and a scientific internship. This example selects the extended 30-EC project.
audience.comparisonExplanation: UCR can combine substantial biology, neuroscience, psychology and empirical methods. Its options prioritise a broad brain-and-behaviour response, cognition and computational analysis, or biological mechanisms and disease. UvA provides a more prescribed experimental sequence and a required psychobiological internship; the relationships shown are partial.

componentNotes.y2-06: The programming practical is completed before Experimental Psychology, as strongly recommended. Experimental Psychology and programming precede the EEG practical.

componentNotes.y2-12: Experimentation — Neurophysiology is the current name of the former Hodgkin & Huxley and Neuropharmacology practical; both names refer to the same requirement.
componentNotes.y3-01: Thirty EC remain open for approved electives, a minor or exchange. No particular course or host is assumed. At most 12 EC of the elective space may be introductory first-year courses; outside courses require advance approval and must avoid excessive overlap. All first-year courses must be passed before third-year programme electives.
componentNotes.y3-02: This example selects the permitted extended 30-EC scientific internship/project. Entry requires 120 EC one month before starting, including the full first year, Philosophy of Science and Statistical Reasoning, the second-year review and all five experimental practicals: programming, experimental psychology, EEG, molecular cell biology and neurophysiology. Completing both earlier years meets these conditions. The project includes supervised original research, an English scientific report and an English presentation; no host or research topic is assumed.

ACCPPDE101.name: Personal & Professional Development
ACCPPDE101.text: This course is a first-year requirement and aims to stimulate personal development, namely, being able to actively, consciously and ethically orientate oneself in relation to others and the world. It supports the development of core personal and academic skills that enhance critical thinking and independent learning. It seeks to improve and develop academic writing and presenting skills and helps students develop the foundational skills and attitudes to reflect on societal issues and engage with societal partners.

BENGATE102.name: Research Methods & Statistics
BENGATE102.text: Research Methods & Statistics introduces research design, operationalisation, measurement, sampling, surveys and experiments. Students study descriptive statistics, estimation, hypothesis testing and introductory regression using R and R Commander. A group project develops a research plan and instruments, collects and analyses data, and reports findings under research-ethics and privacy requirements.

DISARIN211.name: Decision-making in AI
DISARIN211.text: Decision-making in AI examines how intelligent agents make decisions under uncertainty. Students study probability, Bayesian networks, temporal models, expected utility, Markov decision processes, partial observability and bandit problems. Multi-agent decisions and probabilistic programming extend the analysis, supported by equations, numerical examples and scientific papers.

DISARIN212.text: Introduces formal logic, abstract reasoning and proof. Students work with propositions, quantified statements, sets, Boolean algebra, functions and relations, direct and indirect proofs, induction and recursion. A final component models processes and games without chance and investigates winning strategies.

Topics include uninformed and heuristic search, local and global optimisation, adversarial search, constraint satisfaction, linear programming and discrete optimisation. Laboratory exercises and projects develop algorithm implementation, evaluation and experimental investigation of small intelligent systems.

HCBCOGN312.name: Psycholinguistics
HCBCOGN312.text: Psycholinguistics is the study of the neurobiological and psychological factors that enable us to acquire, use, and understand language. Modern research draws on cognitive psychology, neuroscience, and computer science to investigate how language is processed. The course focuses primarily, though not exclusively, on the neuroscience of language. Students examine theoretical and experimental issues in speech production and comprehension, language impairments, the relationship between thought and language, and the evolution and acquisition of language. They also gain hands-on experience with experimental approaches to the study of language and develop an understanding of human linguistic capacity as a subject of multidisciplinary research. Topics covered: What is language? Evolutionary aspects of language and animal communication; language and thought; aphasia; language acquisition; bilingualism; speech comprehension; semantics; reading and dyslexia; speech production.
